About this report
4 July 2025
Manawa Energy Limited (Manawa Energy) presents its Climate-related 
Disclosure for the year ended 31 March 2025 (FY25).
2025 (FY25).
This document has been prepared in accordance, and complies, with Part 7A of 
the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 (FMCA) and the Aotearoa New Zealand 
Climate Standards (NZ CS) published by the External Reporting Board (XRB), 
and forms the climate-related disclosure for Manawa Energy Limited (Manawa 
Energy or the Group) for the FY25 reporting period (Climate Statement). 
This Climate Statement is for the financial period of 1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025.
This Climate Statement has been structured in accordance with NZ CS 1.
Manawa Energy has elected to use several of the adoption provisions in NZ CS 2, 
namely Adoption Provision 2 (Anticipated Financial Impacts), Adoption Provision 4 
(Scope 3 GHG Emissions), Adoption Provision 5 (Comparatives for Scope 3 
Emissions), Adoption Provision 6 (Comparatives for Metrics), Adoption Provision 7 
(Analysis of Trends) and Adoption Provision 8 (Assurance of Scope 3 GHG Emissions).
Reporting Entity
Under Part 7A of the FMCA, Manawa Energy is a climate reporting entity (CRE) 
for the FY25 period and is required to publish climate-related disclosures as part 
of our FY25 reporting.  
This Climate Statement is a group Climate Statement for the purposes of Part 7A 
of the FMCA. References to Manawa Energy include its subsidiaries, as they are  
dentified at page 38 of the FY25 Annual Report available on our website (referred 
to throughout this report as “Manawa”, “Manawa Energy”, “our” or “we”). The scope 
of the reporting entity aligns with that used for Manawa Energy’s FY25 Group 
Financial Statements, which are located in its 2025 Annual Report (pages 46 to 75). 
Financial numbers, as presented in this Climate Statement are in New Zealand 
dollars (NZD) and rounded to millions ($m), unless otherwise stated. In some 
instances, quantifications have been provided as a range.  
Unless otherwise expressly stated, where external documents are referred to 
in this Climate Statement (for example, our FY25 Annual Report), these do not 
form part of the disclosures but are simply general and/or contextual information 
to direct the reader to further information, should they wish to read more.
A glossary of key terms and acronyms referred to in this Climate Statement is 
included at page 69.
A Limited Assurance Opinion over Scope 1 and Scope 2 greenhouse gas (GHG) 
emissions is included at pages 70 to 72.

Important Notice 
This group Climate Statement contains current and 
forward-looking statements about climate change 
and the current and anticipated future impacts of 
climate change on Manawa Energy Limited (Manawa 
Energy). These forward-looking statements include 
(but are not limited to) climate-related scenarios, 
climate-related risks and opportunities (CRROs), 
anticipated impacts, and transition plan actions.
The statements in this document (including 
those which are forward-looking) are based on 
assumptions, estimates, and judgements that are 
uncertain and subject to change. They should not 
be taken as guarantees of future performance 
and the reader should note there are many factors 
(climatic, government, technological, and market 
factors) that could cause Manawa Energy’s actual 
results, performance, risks, or opportunities to differ 
materially from those described in this Climate 
Statement. In particular, the CRROs described in this 
Climate Statement may not eventuate, or may be 
more or less significant than anticipated, and there 
could be significant climate-related impacts that 
eventuate, which have not been identified in this 
Climate Statement.
Manawa Energy does not represent that the 
information in this Climate Statement will not 
change following publication and gives no 
undertaking to update the information over time 
(subject to relevant legal or regulatory requirements). 
Nothing in this Climate Statement should be 
interpreted as capital growth, earnings or any other 
legal, financial, tax or other advice or guidance.
Scheme of Arrangement 
On 7 May 2025, after the end of Manawa Energy’s 
financial year (but prior to publication of this Climate 
Statement), the Commerce Commission gave its 
clearance for Contact Energy Limited’s (Contact 
Energy) proposed acquisition of Manawa Energy 
under a Scheme of Arrangement (Scheme).  
At the date of this Climate Statement, the High 
Court has approved the Scheme. The Scheme is set 
to take effect on or around 11 July 2025, subject to all 
remaining conditions of the Scheme being satisfied.
If the Scheme does take effect: 
	› Contact Energy will become the sole shareholder of 
Manawa Energy;
	› Manawa Energy will be delisted from the NZX (that 
is, all Manawa Energy equity and debt securities will 
cease to be quoted on the NZX on, or shortly after, 
the Scheme’s implementation);
	› Manawa Energy will cease to be a listed issuer under 
the Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 (FMCA) 
and will cease to be a climate reporting entity for 
the reporting period commencing 1 April 2025; and
	› The Board of Directors of Manawa Energy will change. 
In this context, and having regard to the uncertainties 
referenced above, readers should note that the 
disclosures in this Climate Statement reflect Manawa 
Energy’s circumstances as they were in the FY25 
reporting period and do not take into account the 
impact that the implementation of the Scheme (if 
completed) and subsequent integration of Manawa 
Energy’s operations into the Contact Energy group, 
including the approach by a new Board of Directors 
to governance, strategy and risk management that 
Contact Energy may bring.
More information about the Scheme (including 
the conditions) is available at https://www.
manawaenergy.co.nz/soa-information.

Message from the Board
Manawa Energy recognises that a changing climate will necessitate 
changes to the way the New Zealand energy sector operates 
and that it will be increasingly important for all energy market 
participants to consider the impacts of climate change on their 
businesses. Those impacts are already creating, and will continue 
to create, both risks and opportunities for Manawa Energy and 
New Zealand’s energy sector generally.   
Changing weather patterns, including an increase in the frequency of extreme 
weather events, are expected to be observed in the near to medium-term future, 
the physical impacts of these weather events – including flooding, high winds, and 
extended dry periods or droughts – will increase the risks to our business. New 
Zealand’s hydropower schemes and other renewable generation assets (including 
solar and wind generation facilities) are all weather reliant and therefore will be 
affected, to some degree, by the weather-related impacts of climate change.  
Manawa Energy’s assets are geographically diverse, which creates a level of 
natural resilience to individual extreme weather events.
The broader efforts to mitigate and adapt to the effects of climate change, such 
as political response or regulatory changes, also present risks and opportunities 
for Manawa Energy. As a large independent power producer, with a high-quality 
development pipeline, we are well positioned to support the national ambition 
for a low-emissions and climate-resilient future. A significant increase in demand 
for renewable electricity is expected as the economy transitions to meet the 
“2050 target” under the Climate Change Response Act 2002, for net zero of all 
GHG emissions (other than biogenic methane by 2050).1 However, the transition 
will bring opportunities and challenges for the sector to resolve necessitating an 
adaptive, resilient approach.
This Climate Statement has been prepared as Manawa Energy itself is going 
through a significant transition – in September 2024, Manawa Energy announced 
it had entered into a Scheme Implementation Agreement with Contact Energy 
Limited under which Contact Energy agreed to acquire all of Manawa Energy’s 
shares through a Scheme of Arrangement (Scheme). At the time of this Climate 
Statement, the Scheme is set to take effect on or around 11 July 2025 (subject 
to all remaining conditions of the Scheme being satisfied). If the Scheme 
does take effect (and once Manawa Energy ceases to be a listed issuer on the 
NZX), Manawa Energy will cease to be a climate reporting entity (CRE) for the 
reporting period commencing 1 April 2025. In this context, we note that the 
disclosures in this Climate Statement reflect Manawa Energy’s circumstances as 
they were in the reporting period and do not take into account the impact that 
implementation of the Scheme (if completed) and subsequent integration of 
Manawa Energy’s operations into the Contact Energy group may have, including 
the approach of a new Board of Directors to governance, strategy and risk 
management that Contact Energy may bring in the future.

Energy by:

Background
This Climate Statement sets out how climate change is currently 
impacting Manawa Energy, as well as identifying the possible 
climate-related risks and opportunities (CRROs) that could impact 
our business in different climate-related scenarios in the future. 
It is designed to facilitate assessments about how Manawa Energy 
is responding to climate change, and how it will do so in the future, 
in order to assess the resilience of our business model and strategy.   
We have had regard to our primary users when preparing this Climate Statement. 
Primary users include existing and potential investors, customers, lenders and 
other creditors, and our wider stakeholders who are all predominantly based in 
New Zealand. Manawa Energy has also considered how our primary users might 
change in the future.
FY25 is the second period during which Manawa Energy has prepared a 
climate-related disclosure in accordance with the NZ CS, with our FY24 Climate 
Statement being our first disclosure under NZ CS. We previously considered 
climate change in our governance, strategy, and risk management approach, 
which included disclosing against the TCFD Framework in FY21 (as Trustpower) 
and in FY22 (as Manawa Energy). We also voluntarily disclosed against aspects of 
the NZ CS in FY23 (see our FY23 Integrated Report available on our website for 
further details). 
In FY23 and FY24, we engaged a climate consultancy to help us prepare for 
reporting against the NZ CS, and in FY25, we engaged external expertise to 
further progress our focus on this important area. This work has not only helped 
us to report against the NZ CS, but also to better understand our risks and 
opportunities in relation to various climate-related scenarios and integrate this 
knowledge and information into our current and future business planning. 
We undertook further foundational work for climate reporting in FY24 – including 
exploring and understanding stakeholder motivations, finalising our Sustainability 
Strategy and Plan, and working to better understand the CRROs for our business, 
and in FY25 we enhanced our GHG reporting by introducing dedicated carbon 
accounting software, quantified the current climate-related impacts on Manawa 
Energy for the reporting year, and developed an initial Transition Plan, setting out 
what we envisage would be our approach to position Manawa Energy to transition 
to a low-emissions, climate-resilient future.

NZCS Compliance and 
Adoption Provisions
This Climate Statement complies with the requirements set out in 
the NZCS issued by the XRB, as they apply in respect of the FY25 
reporting period. 
Manawa Energy has relied on adoption provisions available under NZ CS 2 in 
this second year of reporting, which provide exceptions from NZCS disclosure 
obligations that Manawa Energy would otherwise be required to comply with.
For this FY25 Climate Statement, we have relied upon the following:
Adoption Provisions 2 
Anticipated Financial Impacts
Manawa Energy is relying on Adoption Provision 2 and has not disclosed the 
anticipated financial impacts of CRROs reasonably expected by Manawa Energy, 
and related exempt information. 
Adoption Provision 4 
Scope 3 GHG Emissions
Manawa Energy is relying on Adoption Provision 4 so as not to disclose the 
following Scope 3 GHG emissions categories – purchased goods and services, 
capital goods, employee commuting and downstream leased assets. We have 
continued to refine our Scope 3 emissions data collection in FY25, in order to 
support reporting on these expanded categories in the future.
Adoption Provisions 5 
Comparatives for Scope 3 Emissions
Manawa Energy is relying on Adoption Provision 5 in respect of the Scope 3 
emissions categories that it did not report on in FY24. Manawa Energy has 
provided some comparative data for the categories of Scope 3 emissions that 
it did report on in FY24 and has subsequently reported on in FY25.  
Adoption Provisions 6 
Comparatives for Metrics
Manawa Energy is relying on Adoption Provision 6 and has not fully disclosed 
comparatives for other metrics disclosed in FY24 and subsequently in FY25. 
Comparative information has been disclosed for Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions 
as well as some Scope 3 emissions (as noted above).
Adoption Provision 7 
Analysis of Trends
Manawa Energy is relying on Adoption Provision 7 because while we have made 
initial progress in providing an analysis of trends in this Climate Statement by 
comparing our GHG emissions (Scope 1 and 2 baseline, and Scope 3 selected 
categories) for FY24 with our FY25 emission profile, and provided commentary 
on reasons for increases and decreases (as appropriate). A longer data set would 
be required to analyse trends in our emissions profile, over time. We have not 
provided an analysis of trends for other metrics outside of GHG emissions.
Adoption Provision 8 
Assurance of Scope 3 GHG Emissions
Manawa Energy is relying on Adoption Provision 8, such that while its Scope 1 
and Scope 2 GHG emissions have been the subject of a third-party assurance 
engagement, although its Scope 3 GHG emissions in FY25 have not been the 
subject of third-party assurance. The focus in FY25 has been on refining and 
enhancing data collection processes and integrity, in preparation for a future 
third party assurance engagement, once expanded categories of Scope 3 
emissions are available.

Overview 
The governance diagram below sets out a broad overview of the risk and governance relationships and responsibilities of Manawa Energy’s

Committees, Reporting and Disclosure and Risk Management, are set out in the Manawa Energy Corporate Governance Statement. 
Governance
Manawa Energy Board
The governance body responsible for setting Manawa Energy’s overall strategy, direction, and approach to risks and opportunities. The Board is responsible for 
oversight of Climate-related Risks and Opportunities (CRROs), and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) and for our Sustainability Strategy and Plan. 
There is more information about the role of the Board below.
Audit and Risk Committee (ARC)
The ARC is a standing subcommittee of the Board. The Board has delegated 
specific functions and responsibilities to the ARC with respect to climate-
related disclosures and CRROs, including overseeing CRROs and the 
preparation, verification, and publication of Manawa Energy’s Climate-
Related Disclosures (CRD). There is more information about the roles 
of the ARC below.       
People and Remuneration Committee (PRC)
The PRC is a standing subcommittee of the Board. The PRC has 
specific responsibilities related to remuneration, including the incentive 
arrangements for the Chief Executive and management team, which include 
determining appropriate ESG and climate reporting Key Performance 
Indicators (KPIs) relating to ESG and climate reporting. There is more 
information about the roles of the PRC below.
Executive
Chief Executive and Management Team
The Board (via the ARC) delegates responsibility for assessing and managing CRROs to the management team, which includes the Chief Executive. 
The management team has overall accountability for embedding CRROs into risk management, business strategy and planning, budgeting processes 
and frameworks, and regular reporting to the ARC and Board on those matters. 
Operations
Business Functions
Manawa Energy manages the identification and day-to-day 
management of CRROs on a devolved basis, with accountability for 
specific CRROs allocated to particular business functions and responsible 
members of the management team who then report to general 
managers, who in turn report to the CEO.
Risk Owners
CRROs are identified, and Risk Owners assigned within certain risk categories 
that they have been allocated. Risk Owners are responsible for monitoring 
and managing those CRROs using Totum (Manawa Energy’s enterprise risk 
management tool).

Board Oversight of CRROs 
Manawa Energy’s Board is the governance body responsible for 
overseeing our approach to climate-related matters. The Board 
Charter sets out the Board’s core roles and responsibilities with 
respect to the approval and monitoring of Climate-related 
Disclosures. These are:
	› ensuring appropriate audit and risk management systems are in place to 
manage risk within the Board’s approved risk framework;
	› adopting appropriate procedures to ensure compliance with all laws, including 
accounting standards (such as the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate Standards, 
NZ CS);
	› overseeing the Company’s commitment to our values, sustainable 
development, the environment and the health and safety of employees, 
contractors and the communities in which Manawa Energy operates; and
	› ensuring that the Board is and remains appropriately skilled to meet the 
changing needs of the Company, consistent with NZX requirements.
With respect to climate change specifically, the Board is ultimately responsible 
for approving and monitoring financial reporting, climate-related disclosures 
(including the oversight of CRROs), and capital management. 
Audit and Risk Committee (ARC) 
The Audit and Risk Committee’s role is to oversee and assist the Manawa Energy 
Board to comply with its legal obligations in relation to risk management 
(including CRROs) and financial reporting. 
The ARC Charter was amended in November 2024 to reflect the specific 
responsibilities that the Board has delegated to the ARC with respect to climate-
related disclosures and climate-related risks and opportunities. These are:
	› Oversee the identification, quantification and monitoring of Climate Related 
Risks & Opportunities (CRROs);
	› Oversee the regular reporting and governance framework for CRROs;
	› Oversee the Basis of Preparation used in Greenhouse Gas reporting;
	› Ensure that management has established an appropriate system of controls 
and management in relation to climate related risks, and record keeping;
	› Review all Climate Related Disclosures (CRDs) and engage with management 
and the assurance provider in relation to the same; and
	› Recommend the annual CRD for approval to the full Board.
The ARC’s general risk management mandate includes climate-related risks. 
The ARC maintains oversight of climate-related risks within the risk parameters 
defined by the Board as part of Manawa Energy’s Enterprise Risk Management 
(ERM) system, as described further in the Risk Management section of this 
Climate Statement. 
Throughout FY25, the ARC assisted the Board in further developing and 
embedding Manawa Energy’s climate reporting processes.
The practice of the ARC has been to meet at least four times per year, and in 
FY25, the ARC met six times, which included additional out of cycle meetings to 
consider climate-related risk and opportunity identification, management and 
reporting, including the quantification of current climate-related impacts and 
transition planning. All Manawa Energy directors (including those that are not 
members of the ARC) have access to ARC papers and a standing invitation to 
attend ARC meetings, where material CRROs are discussed, and attendance by 
other Board members is a regular occurrence. 
The Chair of the ARC reports to the Board, by way of updates at Board meetings 
that follow the relevant ARC meeting, on the content of ARC meetings. This 
includes reporting on enterprise risk updates (including CRROs) that have been 
considered by the ARC.
Board Skills and Competencies
The Board is committed to ensuring that Manawa Energy operates 
responsibly, ethically and in compliance with our company values – 
including in relation to current impacts and CRROs. The Board 
Charter sets out the specific roles and responsibilities of the 
Board as they relate to climate-related matters, as outlined above. 
When the Board is considering appointing a new or replacement director, Manawa 
Energy undertakes a rigorous evaluation process, as set out in the Board Charter.

experience that prospective directors will ideally possess. The climate expertise, 
skills and competencies of prospective directors are considered and evaluated

All newly appointed directors undertake a comprehensive induction, which 
includes site visits to see Manawa Energy’s generation assets and operating 
environments first hand. 
Time has regularly been set aside in Board meetings to upskill directors on

obligations and best practice with respect to climate reporting and climate

used to support their continuous education on matters relevant to their role at 
Manawa Energy.   
The Board has utilised climate-related expertise – both internally and from 
external advisors – to discharge its roles and responsibilities. For example, 
climate-related presentations, legal advice, and reporting on legislative updates 
in the climate space all contribute to the Board’s (and the wider management 
team’s) ongoing education in climate-related matters. Individual Board members 
are also able to access climate-related materials and knowledge via their other 
roles and membership of organisations such as the Institute of Directors, the 
Trans-Tasman Business Circle and Chapter Zero.
The Board Charter includes a requirement to annually review and evaluate Board 
performance. The FY24 externally facilitated Board governance and performance 
review, and the resulting report, provided an assessment of current capability 
against the Board Strategic Skills Matrix and included feedback for individual 
directors and the whole Board. The report served as the cornerstone for Board 
performance and assisted in identifying professional development priorities. 
The FY25 review of Board performance has however been deferred, pending 
implementation of the Scheme.
Governance of Our Strategy and CRROs 
The Board is committed to building a climate-resilient business and 
considers current impacts and CRROs when reviewing, developing, 
and overseeing the implementation of Manawa Energy’s overall 
strategy. As Aotearoa New Zealand’s largest independent electricity 
generator and renewables developer, resilience is embedded in 
Manawa Energy’s core business strategy.
Consideration of CRROs in Strategy Development 
and Review
As described in the Strategy section of this Climate Statement, Manawa Energy 
has reviewed its strategic framework annually, other than in FY25, where the 
review has been deferred until the outcome of the Scheme is finalised. Instead, 
in FY25 the existing strategic framework and sustainability strategy, as set out in 
FY24, has continued to be developed and implemented and a formal Transition 
Plan has been developed. CRROs that were identified and assessed by the 
management team, the ARC and the Board have been considered in terms of 
our transition planning and the preparation of our Transition Plan but were not 
specifically considered as part of our broader strategy (given that this review 
has been deferred for FY25). Had our annual strategy review not been deferred, 
CRROs would have been considered in conjunction with (and weighed against) 
other business and enterprise risks identified through our risk management 
processes, and appropriate changes made to our strategy in response to the risks 
that were decided by the Board as being material.  
All aspects of Manawa Energy’s current and future strategy are impacted by 
CRROs. For example: 
	› Manawa Energy’s assets are predominantly renewable hydro generators, and 
therefore their value is dependent on the weather and is influenced by any 
changes to climate;
	› As a developer of renewable energy assets (including a pipeline of wind and 
solar development projects), Manawa Energy’s growth strategy is aligned with 
key components of the country’s response to reducing emissions, particularly the 
electrification of New Zealand’s economy and large-scale decarbonisation; and 
	› The management of Manawa Energy’s assets is informed by how resilient they 
are to adverse weather and climate change impacts.
The identification and consideration of CRROs is therefore an integral part of 
Manawa Energy’s strategy development and review processes, as described 
further in the Strategy section.
Consideration of other relevant Climate-Related 
Factors in Strategy Review and Development 
In addition to considering CRROs in the strategic planning process, Manawa 
Energy also uses projections of electricity demand growth such as that from 
the Climate Change Commission (CCC) and Transpower to inform our strategic 
planning and decisions. 
Linkage to our Sustainability Strategy and Plan
Manawa Energy is committed to working for the good of our people, our 
environment, our communities and our shareholders. We had previously identified 
and prioritised 15 material initiatives to ensure our sustainability efforts are geared 
towards the most important environmental, social and governance (ESG) areas. 
This includes a specific focus on climate-related business risks (and opportunities).
Our Sustainability Strategy and Plan, as referenced in our FY24 Climate 
Statement and FY24 Integrated Report has also informed decision-making 
on climate-related ESG considerations across Manawa Energy, including by the 
Board, the ARC and the management team. 
An overview of the Sustainability Strategy and Plan is set out on page 25 of 
our FY25 Annual Report. In relation to climate change specifically, key areas of 
consideration and focus from a governance perspective have included renewable 
energy development, resilience of existing assets and climate related business 
risk (and opportunities). Initiatives that have been undertaken to progress our 
Sustainability Strategy in FY25 generally are described further at pages 25 to 30 
of our FY25 Annual Report.

Governance

Metrics and Targets
Asset Management and its relevance to Strategy 
Manawa Energy’s existing asset strategy centres on the ongoing reliability, safety 
and profitability of our 26 generation schemes. 
Each year, Manawa Energy reviews our asset management plans (AMPs) for each 
of our generation assets. In addition, as part of Manawa Energy’s dam safety 
program, hydrology models for each hydro catchment are routinely reviewed, to 
take account of the latest weather modelling and any recent extreme weather 
events. Any notable changes in rainfall patterns and hydrology are captured 
during this process. These changes identify risks to assets from extreme weather 
events and inform how Manawa Energy’s maintenance budget is spent, as well 
as identifying opportunities to capture additional revenue caused by increased 
rainfall.  
These processes help Manawa Energy to not only identify and integrate current 
impacts and CRROs into strategic planning, but to also understand the overall 
resilience of our assets to climate change and the counter-measures Manawa 
Energy might need to undertake – now and in the future – to sustain that 
resilience. This is reflected in our FY25 Transition Plan, as of 31 March 2025 
(page 49), and further definition of capital deployment in FY25 relating to 
new development, major capital projects and remedial works associated with 
climate-related events is set out in the Metrics and Targets section of this 
Climate Statement.
Understanding CRROs for future Strategy 
Consideration 
Manawa Energy has over the past two years, engaged external expertise to upskill 
and build Manawa Energy’s capability in relation to identifying and assessing 
CRROs. These external advisors work with an internal project team, to engage our 
people, deepen our in-house expertise and further our climate-related work. The 
scenario analysis process that Manawa Energy undertook to prepare the Strategy 
section of this Climate Statement is intended to serve as a valuable input into 
future strategy and overall risk identification and management processes, as 
appropriate, in light of the Scheme with Contact Energy. 
Metrics and Targets for Managing CRROs 
Manawa Energy currently has the following metrics for managing 
CRROs: 
	› Greenhouse gas emissions inventory; 
	› Sustainable Finance Framework;
	› Issuance of energy products such as Renewable Energy Certificates (RECs);
	› Our electricity generation intensity; 
	› Major capital project asset upgrade expenditure; 
	› Expenditure on specific remedial works in response to extreme weather 
events; and
	› Planned new renewable energy development expenditure.    
Prior to the Scheme, we had intended to consider implementing further metrics 
and targets for managing CRROs as part of the climate and sustainability-related 
aspects of Manawa Energy’s strategy and business operations. 
Manawa Energy’s Board oversees the progress and achievement of metrics for 
managing CRROs through various measures, as follows:

Overview of Scenario Analysis Process for FY25
Manawa Energy understands the importance of scenario analysis in 
identifying CRROs, to inform our strategy and business model and 
to assess how resilient our strategy and business model are now and 
will be in the future. 
 We have revised how scenario analysis is prepared and used in this Climate 
Statement compared to FY24. This year we utilised the Aotearoa Circle 
Energy Sector Climate Change Scenarios (Energy Sector Scenarios) as the 
foundation for our own scenario analysis. This contrasts with the more bespoke, 
independently developed, approach used in FY24.
We have adapted the Energy Sector Scenarios as we consider they represent a 
respected, robust and transparent energy industry standard for climate scenarios 
– they have collated a range of reliable sources of data and produced a set of 
scenarios using the framework and methodology recommended by the External 
Reporting Board (XRB). Alignment with these scenarios enables readers to have a 
degree of assurance that the scenarios we have used are consistent with industry 
standards and, potentially (subject to their own approach to scenario analysis), 
our peers in the industry. For these reasons it was decided that this approach 
would provide additional value compared to the approach used in FY24 (and 
therefore, more than offsetting any benefits associated with using a consistent 
scenario analysis from year-to-year).
We have then built upon the foundation provided by the Energy Sector Scenarios 
by applying more granular detail on specific areas that are most critical to Manawa 
Energy’s business. This process primarily used the judgement of internal subject 
matter experts with the results validated via several workshops with internal 
stakeholders and external advisors. The external advisors also helped guide the 
scenario analysis process to ensure consistency with NZ CS requirements and 
related XRB and FMA guidance.4
At a high-level, our FY25 scenario analysis process was structured as follows:  
	› The management team engaged a specialist contractor to Manawa Energy 
(Sustainz Business Solutions), to assume the role of Acting ESG Manager and 
lead the process of developing this Climate Statement and associated CRD 
processes, including scenario analysis and CRRO identification and assessment; 
	› The ARC and the Board received periodic updates on, and contributed 
periodically to, the scenario analysis process – at both scheduled meetings and 
through a series of additional out of cycle meetings to discuss matters specific 
to the CRDs. For example, this included approving an overall project plan, the 
planned approach for scenario analysis, advising on ad hoc queries as and when 
necessary, reviewing the outputs from the scenario analysis and transition 
4	 The external advisors used were Sustainz Business Solutions Limited and Gun Metal Grey Limited.
planning processes, financial quantification of current impacts and approving 
this Climate Statement; and
	› An internal project team (Project Team) was assembled to participate in a 
series of six workshops run internally. The substantive scenario analysis was 
undertaken at these workshops, with outcomes documented and validated.
The workshops broadly followed the structure recommended in the XRB’s Staff 
Guidance for Entity Scenario Development and involved the following key steps: 
	› Step 1: Set the scene, create a project group, and define objectives, milestones, 
and deliverables; 
	› Step 2: Define the focal question, map the value chain and organisational 
boundary, define time horizons; 
	› Step 3: Identify driving forces and critical uncertainties; 
	› Step 4: Select temperature outcomes and emissions pathways; 
	› Step 5: Prepare draft narratives, based on The Aotearoa Circle Energy Sector 
Climate Change Scenarios but taking into account of Manawa Energy’s critical 
drivers and uncertainties as described in more detail below (Manawa Energy 
Scenarios – Interpretation of the Energy Sector Climate Change Scenarios); and 
	› Step 6: Conduct scenario analysis (using a ‘coordinated effort’ 1.5°C scenario, 
a ‘trailblazers’ 2.2°C, a ‘slow followers’ 2.5°C and a ‘hot house’ ≥3.3°C scenario) 
and identify Manawa Energy’s CRROs, taking into account Manawa Energy’s 
climate change scenario narratives, as developed and described in further detail 
below (Manawa Energy Scenarios – Interpretation of the Energy Sector Climate 
Change Scenarios). Through engagement with a multi-disciplinary Project 
Team, these scenarios were systematically considered, assessed and validated, 
with detailed outcomes from workshops and one-on-one consultations 
recorded across each of the four scenarios. This provided the basis for both 
identifying current impacts and framing the transition and physical climate-
related risks and opportunities, described below. 
Final CRRO disclosures were then developed, reviewed by the ARC, finalised and 
provided to the Board for approval.
The scenarios used have not been integrated within Manawa Energy’s strategy 
process to date, as the strategic plan and other strategic processes were deferred 
in FY25 (as described above).

The scenarios described below align with scenario architectures and time horizons 
used in wider energy sector scenario analysis. While they have been specifically 
aligned to the Aotearoa Circle Energy Sector Scenarios, they have considered 
other external views on future climate scenarios, including the scenarios chosen

	› The Aotearoa Circle Energy Sector Climate Change Scenarios, 2024;

to the physical climate;

the 1.5°C, 2.2°C, 2.5°C and ≥3.3°C scenarios respectively;

Manawa Energy Climate Statement FY25
22
Governance
Strategy
Risk Management
Metrics and Targets
Scenario Narratives and Key Issues and Assumptions
Warming to ≥3.3°C by 2080 – Hothouse
Warming to 2.5oC by 2080 – Slow Followers
Both global and domestic emissions reduction initiatives fail, with emissions continuing 
to rise throughout the century. The global temperature climbs beyond 3.3°C by 2080, 
pushing the Earth past critical ecological tipping points. Sea level rise accelerates, 
storm intensity worsens, and extreme heat becomes more frequent. For New Zealand, 
the physical consequences are severe with rainfall becoming increasingly intense and 
unpredictable. These physical changes create compounding stress on natural systems 
and critical infrastructure.
Against this backdrop, precipitation-related impacts become deeply disruptive for the 
energy sector. Torrential rain and flooding regularly damage critical infrastructure – both 
here and abroad. Hydroelectric schemes – traditionally a cornerstone of New Zealand’s 
renewable electricity – struggle with erratic inflows, as droughts interrupt generation 
capacity in summer and extreme weather events lead to increased spill and operational 
instability in winter. Chronic impacts of increased temperatures become material issues 
– aspects such as weed growth in storage lakes and other ecological changes shift from 
manageable to major ongoing issues. The sector’s ability to recover from shocks is 
diminished by political inaction and fragmented adaptation efforts.
New Zealand drags its feet while the rest of the world makes uneven progress on 
climate action. While global emissions peak around 2040, New Zealand remains 
politically cautious, adopting a “bare minimum” approach to climate regulation. 
Domestic policy is slow to evolve, shaped more by economic pressure than proactive 
climate response. Regulation of the electricity sector lacks coherence and ambition, 
creating a reactive and fragmented landscape. Some investors and trade partners begin 
to penalise New Zealand’s inaction, and the country becomes increasingly isolated from 
global green finance and technology flows.
Physically, the country still faces a rise in global temperature of around 2.5°C by 2080. 
Significant, but manageable physical changes in the environment emerge, putting 
increasing pressure on critical infrastructure. These changes are less extreme than in 
Hot House but still significant (and similar, but slightly worse, than that observed in 
Trailblazers). For the electricity sector, the precipitation impacts include more frequent 
and damaging storms, with infrastructure repeatedly hit by heavy rain and wind. Rainfall 
variability makes water storage planning for hydroelectric schemes more difficult, and 
summer droughts threaten the stability of peak-season supply. The lack of investment 
in adaptive infrastructure means the system becomes more brittle over time. Repair 
costs rise, grid reliability drops and while the continuation of thermal generation makes 
long-term management of the system easier, short-term interruptions become more 
common.
Key Issues and Assumptions: 
	› Renewable demand: Low, with thermal generation expected to play a role throughout 
the century.
	› Political and regulatory environment: Hands off regulatory approach, very little in 
the way of intervention, and any interventions likely to be unfavourable for Manawa 
Energy (i.e. supportive of non-renewable technologies).
	› Physical impacts (hydro fuel): Very large changes to inflows in the long-term. Key 
change being significant increase in volatility and inflows become “spikier” – that is, 
droughts last longer with shorter, more intense inflow events. Seasonality of inflows 
shifts to being more winter favoured and drier summer/autumn periods. Any absolute 
change to inflows is assumed to be too uncertain to predict, but possible inflows may 
increase in this scenario (conversely, they may also decrease, but this is less likely). 
	› Physical impacts (extreme weather): Very large increase in storminess in the long-
term with regular extreme weather events that have potential to do localised 
damage.
Key issues and Assumptions:
	› Renewable demand: Moderate to low; much the same as we see now – no direct 
support and thermal generation expected to play a role in the short-term.
	› Political and regulatory environment: Hands off regulatory approach, very little in 
the way of intervention, and any interventions likely to be unfavourable for Manawa 
Energy (i.e. supportive of non-renewable technologies). Slightly less hands-off than 
Hot House.
	› Physical impacts (hydro fuel): Large changes to inflows in the long-term. Similar 
effects to Hot House but lower magnitude changes, similar to that observed in 
Trailblazers (see below). 
	› Physical impacts (extreme weather): Large increase in storminess in the long-term 
with increased (but not continuous or expected every year like Hot House scenario) 
risk of extreme weather events that have potential to do localised damage (e.g. much 
in the way Cyclone Gabrielle was). Effectively little difference between this scenario 
and Trailblazers.

text:
Manawa Energy Climate Statement FY25
23
Governance
Strategy
Risk Management
Metrics and Targets
Warming Limited to 2.2°C by 2080 – Trailblazers
Warming Limited to 1.5°C by 2080 – Coordinated Effort
New Zealand becomes a proactive climate leader, implementing bold domestic 
policy even as global efforts remain fragmented. Electricity regulation is focussed 
on decarbonisation goals, despite reluctance from some parts of the international 
community. Incentives for electrification create a supportive domestic policy 
environment for innovation and adaptation. However, transition risks emerge from 
the pace and scale of change, and from a lack of international coherence that drives 
up the cost of low-carbon technologies and limits cross-border cooperation.
The physical world in this scenario is less volatile than in the previous two, but still 
deeply affected. Temperatures rise by around 2.2°C by 2080. Sea level rise and extreme 
weather events continue, though more slowly, though similar to that observed in the 
Slow Followers scenario. Rainfall becomes less predictable, especially in the timing and 
intensity of seasonal flows. For hydro-dependent generation, this presents a nuanced 
challenge: in the South Island, increased winter rainfall helps reduce pressure during 
peak heating demand, but drier summers stretch storage capacity and complicate 
generation planning. Intense rain events and storms still damage assets and disrupt 
service, making ongoing adaptation essential.
The energy system has invested in resilience, with better forecasting, smart 
infrastructure, and diversified energy sources that help mitigate the volatility, 
but this is limited to known technologies, and the industry continues to be relatively risk 
averse in the context of application of advanced tech, relying on the “tried and true”. 
The world comes together to aggressively decarbonise, with global and New Zealand 
policy ambition at its highest. Emissions peak in the 2020s and fall to net zero by 
the 2050s. The electricity sector in New Zealand is highly regulated and supported 
by a coherent and stable policy framework. The Emissions Trading Scheme (ETS) is 
functioning effectively, long-term planning is embedded in infrastructure regulation, 
and cross-sector coordination ensures that new technologies are deployed efficiently. 
Energy equity, climate resilience, and emissions reduction are pursued simultaneously, 
enabling both public and private investment in a low-carbon future.
Physically, this is the least damaging climate pathway, though impacts still materialise. 
Global temperature rise is limited to around 1.5°C, but even under this scenario, New 
Zealand faces more hot days, increased rainfall intensity, and rising sea levels. For the 
electricity sector, this means a more manageable – but still significant – change in 
hydrological patterns. Enhanced winter rainfall helps with hydro generation during 
winter, but long, dry, periods still increase in frequency compared to what has been 
historically observed. Extreme weather events are still observed but are less frequent 
and therefore more manageable.
The investment community actively responds to the challenges of climate change 
– renewable investments are prioritised, and the integration challenges renewable 
growth bring are tackled with advances in technology and universal willingness to 
step away from fossil fuels, regardless of the costs. The system is not immune to the 
changes and challenges, but it has the tools and coordination to bounce back quickly, 
and diversification (both geographic, and in terms of generation type) are likely to be 
important considerations.
Key issues and Assumptions: 
	› Renewable demand: Moderate; similar to what we see now but political support for 
renewables is much more favourable. Noting this favourability may not translate to 
greater support/increased demand due to unintended consequences and other sub-
optimal policy outcomes.
	› Political and regulatory environment: Local regulatory environment very supportive 
of decarbonisation and renewable generation, with direct intervention possible (but 
not as likely/well designed as Coordinated Effort). Likely some interventions will be 
reactive rather than planned (i.e. knee-jerk reactions to disruptive events)
	› Physical impacts (hydro fuel): Moderate to large changes to inflows in the long-term. 
Similar effects to Hot House and Slow Followers but lower magnitude changes.
	› Physical impacts (extreme weather): Large increase in storminess in the long-term 
with increased (but not continuous or expected every year like Hot House scenario) 
risk of extreme weather events that have potential to do localised damage. Effectively 
little difference between this scenario and Slow Followers. 
Key Issues and Assumptions: 
	› Renewable demand: High demand supported by public and private sectors highly 
motivated to decarbonise. Unlike Trailblazers, it is expected this drive to decarbonise 
isn’t just Government or Regulatory mandated, but organically driven by lower costs, 
unequivocal public support and advances in technology.
	› Political and regulatory environment: Highly supportive environment for renewables, 
with bipartisan support for relevant policies. Policies are more carefully considered and 
assumed to have less unintended consequences (as this scenario is “planned” rather 
than “reactive”).
	› Physical impacts (hydro fuel and extreme weather): Little change – no changes 
beyond what we currently observe (which, notably, aren’t zero, just difficult to predict 
with any certainty).

Manawa Energy’s Climate-related Risks and Opportunities
In FY25, we updated the time horizons that we considered for the identification and assessment of our CRROs and aligned with those used within the Aotearoa Circle 
Energy Sector Climate Change Scenario work, with the exception of extending the long-term time horizon out to 2100. These time horizons make sense to Manawa 
Energy in terms of consenting new generation development and long-term asset management for our long-lived assets. 
Time Horizons for CRROs
Horizon
Period
Description
Short-term 
2024–2030
Reflects the timeframe of New Zealand’s first two emissions budgets and aligned with Manawa Energy’s near-
term strategic goals.
	› This represents the immediate near-term environment where planning artifacts (Business Strategy, Asset Management Plan, 
etc.) are largely fixed with many details known.
	› We have a good understanding of what to expect in this time frame, with key sources of uncertainty largely around “when” 
and “how” rather than “what” – that is, our strategy in this timeframe is well defined and has specific targets, including a robust 
capital plan to maintain existing assets and execute on growth ambitions.
	› In this time frame, we do not expect a significant shift in the physical impacts of climate change from what we observe today.
Medium-term 
2031–2050
Aligned with key targets and milestones set for 2050, including Paris Agreement emission reduction plans.
	› This represents the period where the sector is expected to evolve and change rapidly, with many of the driving forces largely 
settled (e.g. ETS is in place with the framework largely expected to be stable despite the cyclical nature of political and market 
conditions); yet the specifics and inevitable disruptions are very uncertain and very difficult to predict with any kind of certainty.
	› This timeframe covers the transition from a strategy that contains specific targets and goals to a lesser defined set of ambitions. 
	› The level of uncertainty in the medium- and long-term necessitates developing a strategy and capital plan that is resilient to a 
range of possible outcomes rather than a specific “to-do list”. 
	› This time frame is where we expect to see the divergence of physical impacts between different scenarios – with some scenarios 
assuming the emergence of the more severe physical risks.
Long-term 
2051–2100
Aligned with the long-life nature of energy sector assets.
	› This represents an outer horizon where no specifics are known and the value of having a range of different scenarios 
comes into play: it is useful to understand the continuum of effects in these scenarios in order to develop least regrets 
plans (especially important given the long-life nature of energy assets)
	› In this time frame the scenarios, and hence our strategic planning for each of these scenarios, are vastly different from 
one another – the higher temperature scenarios realising the full suite of anticipated consequences of climate change, 
while the lower temperature scenarios are more a continuation of the types of impacts we see today.
	› Due to the extreme amount of uncertainty in this timeframe, strategic and capital planning is more difficult; however, 
given the nature of our assets, we need to think about how each scenario will affect our assets.
 
These time horizons are broadly consistent with strategic planning and capital deployment time frames, with the current strategy focused primarily on short-term 
and medium-term considerations (i.e. next 5 years, next 25 years), but extends into the long-term when deploying capital as we are investing in long-life assets.

Our changing climate will undoubtedly shape the way Manawa 
Energy operates in the medium- to long-term, and we know more 
extreme weather patterns could increase the risk of damage to 
our assets and impact our generation revenue both positively and 
negatively.
Our existing asset management planning and our future renewable development 
strategy, together with the work we have undertaken to prepare our first 
Transition Plan within this Climate Statement, positions us to manage climate-
related risk, leverage climate-related opportunities, and build a more climate-
resilient business going forward. 
For our first reporting period under the climate-related disclosures regime 
in FY24, Manawa Energy relied on Adoption Provision 3, while indicating that 
Manawa Energy was in the process of developing the transition plan aspects of 
our strategy. In FY25, we have developed an initial Transition Plan. This sets out 
key areas of focus and priorities for leveraging opportunities, managing risks, and 
delivering climate ambition and capability across the time horizons of Manawa 
Energy today, near term actions (to 2030), and future state (from 2031 and 
beyond), to ultimately position Manawa Energy to transition to a low-emissions, 
climate-resilient future, as assessed for the Company as structured and operating 
at the end of FY25.
As with any plan, Manawa Energy’s Transition Plan is subject to change, but 
readers should note that the Scheme could have a particularly significant impact 
depending on the priorities of Manawa Energy’s Board following implementation 
of the Scheme. Nevertheless, in developing this Transition Plan, we have focussed 
on aligning plans to commercial drivers, to seek to focus on initiatives that may 
have the broad support of future stakeholders.
A key consideration in developing the Transition Plan has been how Manawa 
Energy would continue to operate, generate sustainable revenue, protect our 
assets and finance our business in a low-emissions, climate-resilient future, while 
acknowledging that as a renewable energy generator, resilience to physical risks 
is already inherently embedded in our business strategy. By its nature, this has 
included balancing short-term and long-term tensions, setting out tangible 
actions, where we can. It is recognised that this is a dynamic and iterative process, 
where uncertainty is embraced and planned for, and assumptions are tested.
In developing this Transition Plan, we have considered the mandatory 
requirements of the NZ CS, the expectations of key stakeholders (including 
intended primary users of Manawa Energy’s Climate Statement) and integration 
with Manawa Energy’s core business and ESG strategies and plans. This work 
was also informed by the scenario analysis work (described above), and we 
make specific reference to relevant CRROs, where appropriate, in our Transition 
Plan. Scoping and definition were further informed by a transition plan maturity 
assessment (maturity assessment).

could be considered as transition planning efforts, identified gaps in those 
measures, and highlighted key areas for development in terms of the transition to 
a climate-resilient future state. This included consideration of the scope of recent 
Manawa Energy disclosures, the extent to which, and how these could link with 
and inform the Transition Plan, and those areas where integration with existing 
Manawa Energy strategies, frameworks and plans could be further developed or 
reinforced.

The aspects of the Transition Plan relating to “Manawa Today” have been 
integrated into internal capital deployment and funding decision-making 
processes.

The identification, assessment and management of climate-related risks and

We identify and assess climate-related risks in the same way we identify and 
assess other types of enterprise risk, using our ERM system and the other risk

FY25 Scenario Analysis Process for Identifying and Assessing 
Climate-related Risks and Opportunities
For our second reporting period under the climate-related disclosures regime, 
the Strategy section of this Climate Statement includes further details about the 
scenario analysis process that we used to identify and consider CRROs in FY25. 
This includes definition of: 
	› the specific climate-related scenarios considered;

incorporated within internal risk management and capital deployment and 
assisted with developing informed climate-related risk strategy and adaptation 
management. This is described further in the Metrics and Targets section of

To inform interpretation of these results, an overview and comparison of GHG 
emission results for FY25 relative to the base year (FY24 in relation to Scope 1 and 2 
emissions) is provided below: 
Scope 1 – An increase of 175% between FY24 and FY25 emissions is attributable 
to the following: 
	› A 709% increase in stationary combustion is due to the dry-calm winter in 
2024 resulting in an energy shortage across the country and Manawa Energy’s 
portfolio, leading to higher utilisation of the Bream Bay thermal peaker plant. 
This was also reflected in a significantly higher proportion of thermal generation 
utilisation across New Zealand over this period. In addition, Bream Bay was used 
as cover during an extended, unplanned outage in Northland in June 2024, 
following the collapse of a Transpower pylon, providing essential back-up power 
supply while transmission lines were reinstated; 
	› A marginal increase of 3.5% in relation to the mobile fleet indicates the fleet 
remained relatively unchanged, and while some swings in certain drivers was 
experienced, on the whole, no behavioural or organisational changes occurred 
between FY24 and FY25; and 
	› A 100% decrease in refrigerants relates to a change from the average leakage 
rate calculation to the top-up method, as a more accurate measure, based on 
actual refrigerant usage.  
Scope 2 – A decrease of between 19.5% (market based) and 20% (location based) 
is attributable to:  
	› Purchased electricity decreasing due to a lower level of pumping at the 
Highbank scheme during the irrigation season. The extremely wet December 
2024 and January 2025 conditions in Canterbury meant that demand from 
irrigators was reduced, with water availability in races being sufficient to meet 
demand, reducing the need for pumping in January and March 2025.

attributable to:

as described above;

emissions, due to lower staff numbers and less waste produced at Manawa 
Energy sites; and

Remuneration 
Refer to the Governance section of this Climate Statement (CRRO Management 
Performance Linked to Remuneration), for the remuneration of Manawa Energy’s 
Chief Executive and Executive Team that is linked to Manawa Energy’s shared 
Company goals, including those that are climate-related. This is subject to review 
on an annual basis. 
The initial Transition Plan, as of 31 March 2025, included a near-term goal of 
reviewing executive and management remuneration incentives by 2030, to ensure 
these reflect appropriate climate-related metric(s) in line with Manawa Energy’s 
business strategy and objectives, at that time.
Exposure to Risks and Opportunities and 
the Impact of the Changing Climate on 
Manawa Energy’s Assets and Business  
Manawa Energy’s current business operations and our future strategy, as 
described in the Strategy section of this Climate Statement, are impacted 
by CRROs in the following ways: 
	› The profitability of all Manawa Energy’s existing assets is heavily impacted by 
the weather and, transition responses to climate change, as such, vulnerable to 
the transition and physical risks associated with climate change; and
	› As a renewable energy developer Manawa Energy’s growth strategy is aligned 
with New Zealand’s electrification and decarbonisation goals. All of Manawa 
Energy’s existing assets, new development and future strategy present an 
opportunity to contribute to large-scale decarbonisation of New Zealand’s 
economy.
Due to the nature of Manawa Energy’s business, its operations, assets, and 
business activities are affected by changes to the climate and the specific CRROs 
that arise out of those changes. Manawa Energy has therefore determined that:
	› Transition risks: All (100%) of our existing and development assets are 
vulnerable to the transition risks of climate change, including in particular, 
regulatory and policy change, a key transition risk facing all energy 
sector participants. If regulatory change negatively impacts electricity 
generation, then this also impacts the revenue we can generate from our 
existing generation assets and may also negatively impact the value of our 
development options. Equally, if we cannot access the necessary resources and 
infrastructure from both global and domestic markets to progress our pipeline 
projects, our business activities will be significantly impacted; 
	› Physical risks: All (100%) of Manawa Energy’ s existing hydro generation assets 
are (to a greater or lesser extent) vulnerable to the physical risks of climate 
change; and  
	› Climate-related opportunities: 	Conversely, all (100%) of Manawa Energy’s 
generation assets have (to a greater or lesser extent) the ability to provide 
options and opportunities in response to climate change and are therefore 
aligned with climate-related opportunities. 
These assessments are the same as they were in FY24.
Climate-Related Targets 
Manawa Energy does not currently have any GHG emissions reduction targets, 
although our Transition Plan describes when these might be developed. 
Manawa Energy has set FY24 as the Base Year for GHG emissions measurement, 
in relation to our Scope 1 and Scope 2 emissions, and in FY25, continued to further 
evaluate our emissions profile, with a view to finalising our emissions reduction 
plan and positioning the Company for setting future targets. Manawa Energy 
engaged external expertise to assist with this process. We have been considering 
the Science Based Target Initiative (SBTi) framework to inform possible options 
for emissions targets including emissions intensity approach, along with a 
science-aligned approach, although this work was deferred for FY25 in light 
of the Scheme.
We consider that emissions intensity targets would best align with Manawa 
Energy’s strategy for enhancing our existing assets and developing our new 
renewable generation, and while in FY25 specific targets had yet to be defined, 
our initial Transition Plan (as of 31 March 2025), included reference to the future 
definition of climate-related targets, as a near-term action, intended to be in 
place by 2030. 
Manawa Energy has not used emissions offsets for FY25 and does not currently 
have any plans to use offsets for FY26 or subsequent financial years.

Glossary and 
Acronyms1
Adaptation
Changes in processes, practices and 
structures to moderate potential 
damage or to benefit from 
opportunities associated with 
climate change.
Aotearoa New Zealand Climate 
Standards (NZCS)
Standards issued by the XRB that 
comprise the New Zealand climate-
related disclosure framework. These 
include NZ CS 1, NZ CS 2 and NZ CS 3. 
CREs are required to report against 
these standards. It includes requirements 
to disclose information about exposure 
to climate-related risks and opportunities 
(applies to around 200 economically 
significant entities in New Zealand). 
Carbon Capture Utilisation and 
Storage (CCUS)
Involves the capture of carbon dioxide 
(O2) generally from large point sources 
like power generation or industrial 
facilities that use either fossil fuels or 
biomass as fuel. If not being used on-
site, the captured CO2 is compressed 
and transported by pipeline, ship, 
rail or truck to be used in a range of 
applications or injected into deep 
geological formations such as depleted 
oil and gas reservoirs or saline aquifers.2
Climate-Related Disclosure 
Framework
Climate-related disclosure (CRD) 
framework refers to climate statements, 
group climate statements, or other 
information that complies with the 
climate-related disclosure frameworks, 
such as the Aotearoa New Zealand 
Climate Standards. This has the same 
meaning set out in section 9AA of 
the Financial Reporting Act 2013.
Climate-Related Impacts 
The effects (also referred to as 
consequences or outcomes) of 
climate change occurring for an entity. 
These effects will, in turn, depend 
on the impacts of climate change 
on the broader socioeconomic and 
ecological systems an entity operates 
within (including an entity’s value 
chain).	
Climate-Related Opportunity
The potentially positive climate-related 
outcomes for Manawa and can include 
both physical and transition opportunities. 
Efforts to mitigate and adapt to climate 
change can produce opportunities 
for entities, such as through resource 
efficiency and cost savings, the adoption 
and utilisation of low-emissions energy 
sources, the development of new 
products and services, and building 
resilience along the value chain.
Climate-Related Risks
The potential negative impacts of 
climate change on an entity. See 
also definitions of physical risks and 
transition risks. 
Climate Reporting Entity (CRE)
Has the meaning given to that term in 
Section 461O of the Financial Markets 
Conduct Act 2013 (FMC Act), It covers 
large NZ entities with higher levels of 
public accountability than other FMC 
reporting entities and includes large 
banks, insurers, managers of investment 
schemes, and large publicly listed 
entities, including Manawa Energy.
CO2e
The universal unit of measurement to 
indicate the global warming potential 
of each of the seven GHGs, expressed in 
terms of the global warming potential 
of one unit of carbon dioxide for 100 
years. It is used to evaluate releasing (or 
avoiding releasing) any GHGs against a 
common basis.
CRRO
Climate-Related Risks and Opportunities 
(see detailed definitions – Climate-
Related Opportunity, Climate-Related 
Risk, Physical Risks, Transition Risks).
ESG
The environmental, social and governance 
factors to assess sustainability practices 
and performance.
Financial Impacts
The translation of impacts into current 
or anticipated impacts on financial 
performance, financial position and 
cash flows.
FY
The financial year ended 31 March of the 
stated year.
GHG
Greenhouse Gases are the seven gases 
listed in the Kyoto Protocol.3 These GHGs 
are currently carbon dioxide (CO2), 
methane (CH4), nitrous oxide (N2O), 
hydrofluorocarbons (HFCs), 
perfluorocarbons (PFCs), sulphur 
hexafluoride (SF6) and nitrogen 
trifluoride (NF3).	
GHG Protocol
The Greenhouse Gas Protocol, is a 
partnership between World Resources 
Institute (WRI) and the World Business 
Council for Sustainable Development 
(WBCSD). The GHG Protocol develops 
standards and guidance, such as the 
Corporate Standard and the Corporate 
Value Chain Scope 3 Standard, both 
used, as referenced, for Manawa 
Energy’s reporting.
Global Warming Potential (GWP)
A factor describing the radiative 
forcing impact (degree of harm to the 
atmosphere) of one unit of a given GHG 
relative to one unit of carbon dioxide CO2.
Mitigation
Could include mitigation of disaster, 
or of climate change. Mitigation of 
disaster relates to the lessening of the 
potential adverse impacts of physical 
hazards (including those that are human 
induced) through actions that reduce 
hazard, exposure, and vulnerability. 
Mitigation of climate change refers 
to human intervention to reduce 
greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions or 
enhance GHG removals.​
Net Zero
In general terms (but subject to the 
definition used in a particular context), 
a condition in which the amount of 
human-caused residual greenhouse gas 
(GHGs) released are balanced by the 
amount of human-led removal from the 
atmosphere over a specified period and 
within specified boundaries. Achieving 
this balance may involve a combination 
of emission reductions, offsetting (but 
only offsetting that constitutes removal) 
and innovative technologies. ISO Net 
Zero Guidelines (IWA 42.2022)​. In this 
explanation, “balanced” refers to an 
accounting assessment and is not a 
representation that the environment or 
other relevant domains are in balance at 
Net Zero.
NZX
New Zealand Stock Exchange.	
Organisational Boundary
Organisational boundary defines the 
scope within which a company or entity 
operates, establishing the limits for 
responsibilities, control, and operations.​
Physical Risks
Risks related to the physical impacts 
of climate change. Physical risks 
emanating from climate change can be 
event-driven (acute) such as increased 
severity of extreme weather events. 
They can also relate to longer-term 
shifts (chronic) in precipitation and 
temperature and increased variability 
in weather events, such as sea level rise.
Primary Users
Existing and potential investors, lenders 
and other creditors.
Scenario
A plausible, challenging description of 
how the future may develop based on 
a coherent and internally consistent set 
of assumptions about key driving forces 
and relationships, covering both physical 
and transition risks in an integrated 
manner. Climate-related scenarios are 
not intended to be probabilistic or 
predictive, or to identify the ‘most likely’ 
outcome(s) of climate change. They are 
intended to provide an opportunity for 
entities to develop their internal capacity 
to better understand and prepare for 
the uncertain future impacts of climate 
change.
Scenario Analysis
A process for systematically exploring 
the effects of a range of plausible future 
events under conditions of uncertainty. 
Engaging in this process helps an entity 
to identify its climate-related risks and 
opportunities and develop a better 
understanding of the resilience of its 
business model and strategy.
Scheme of Arrangement/Scheme
The agreement/mechanism by which 
Contact Energy Limited may acquire all 
the shares in Manawa Energy Limited as 
described at www.manawaenergy.co.nz/
soa-information.
The Aotearoa Circle Energy Sector 
Climate Change Scenarios
The Energy Sector Scenarios, published 
by the Aotearoa Circle in 2024. 
Represents a comprehensive package 
of strategic analysis that is designed to 
support climate disclosures across the 
energy sector.
Transition Plan
An aspect of the entity’s overall strategy 
that describes targets, including any 
interim targets, and actions for its 
transition towards a low-emissions, 
climate-resilient future.
Transition Risks
Risks related to the transition to a 
low-emissions, climate-resilient global 
and domestic economy, such as policy, 
legal, technology, market and reputation 
changes associated with the mitigation 
and adaptation requirements relating to 
climate change.
Value Chain
The full range of activities, resources 
and relationships related to Manawa 
Energy’s business model and the 
external environment in which it 
operates. It encompasses the activities, 
resources and relationships Manawa 
Energy uses and relies on to create its 
products or services, from conception 
to delivery, consumption and end of 
life (e.g. those in Manawa Energy’s 
operations such as human resource, 
those along its supply chain, marketing 
and distribution channels, and the 
financing, geographical, geopolitical 
and regulatory environments in which 
it operates).
XRB
The External Reporting Board (XRB) 
is an independent Crown Entity that is 
responsible for developing a financial 
reporting strategy for New Zealand, 
preparing and issuing accounting, 
assurance and climate standards and 
non-binding guidance on non-financial 
reporting. 
1	 Terms that are defined in the NZ CS, and used 
in this Climate Statement, have the meaning 
given to them in the NZ CS. 
2	 Carbon Capture Utilisation and Storage 
- Energy System – IEA: www.iea.org/energy-
system/carbon-capture-utilisation-and-
storage
3	 The Kyoto Protocol is an international treaty 
adopted in 1997 and aimed at reducing 
greenhouse gas emissions. It operationalises 
the United Nations Framework Convention 
on Climate Change (UNFCCC) by committing 
industrialised countries and economies to 
transition to limit and reduce greenhouse gas 
emissions in accordance with agreed individual 
targets.

Information subject to assurance
We have performed an engagement to provide limited assurance in relation 
to Manawa Energy Limited’s Scope 1 and 2 Emissions Reporting for the period 
1 April 2024 to 31 March 2025.
Our conclusion on the Scope 1 and 2 Emissions Reporting does not extend to any 
other information included, or referred to, in the climate statements on pages 57 
to 65 or other information that accompanies or contains the climate statement 
and our assurance report (other information). Additionally, our assurance 
engagement does not extend to Scope 3 emissions, of which details may be 
referenced within pages 57 to 65. We have not performed any procedures with 
respect to the other information. 
Criteria
The criteria used as the basis of reporting include the NZ CSs issued by the 
External Reporting Board. As disclosed on pages 57 to 65 of the climate 
statement, the greenhouse gas emissions have been prepared in accordance 
with the World Resources Institute and World Business Council for Sustainable 
Development’s Greenhouse Gas Protocol standards and guidance (collectively, 
the GHG Protocol):  
 
	› Scope 1 emissions have been prepared in accordance with The Greenhouse Gas 
Protocol: A Corporate Accounting and Reporting Standard (revised edition); and
	› Scope 2 emissions have been prepared in accordance with The Greenhouse Gas 
Protocol: GHG Protocol Scope 2 Guidance: An amendment to the GHG Protocol 
Corporate Standard.
As a result, this report may not be suitable for another purpose.
Standards we followed
We conducted our limited assurance engagement in accordance with New Zealand 
Standard on Assurance Engagements 1 (NZ SAE 1) Assurance Engagements over 
Greenhouse Gas Emissions Disclosures and International Standard on Assurance 
Engagements (New Zealand) 3410 Assurance Engagements on Greenhouse Gas

sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our conclusion. 
Our responsibilities under the Standard are further described in the ‘Our 
responsibility’ section of our report. 
Key Matters
We have determined that there are no key matters to communicate in our report.
How to interpret limited assurance and material misstatement
A limited assurance engagement is substantially less in scope than a reasonable 
assurance engagement in relation to both the risk assessment procedures, 
including an understanding of internal control, and the procedures performed 
in response to the assessed risks.
Misstatements, including omissions, within the Scope 1 and 2 Emissions Reporting

be expected to influence the relevant decisions of the intended users taken on

Inherent limitations
As noted in the Scope 1 and 2 Emissions Reporting page 57 to 65, Scope 1 and 2

to combine emissions of different gases. 
Use of this assurance report
Our report is made solely for Manawa Energy Limited. Our assurance work has 
been undertaken so that we might state to Manawa Energy Limited those matters 
we are required to state to them in the assurance report and for no other purpose.
